section: Educational Psychology · Ch7 — Reinforcement Schedules (Complete: FR/VR/FI/VI)
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: A teacher gives a class test every Friday, regardless of how many questions students have practised. Students typically study very little early in the week and cram just before Friday. This weekly-test pattern illustrates a:

options.option_text: Fixed-interval schedule (reinforcement after a fixed, predictable TIME period)

explanation: Fixed-interval schedules reinforce the first response after a fixed, predictable time period — producing the classic 'scalloped' pattern where responding is low right after reinforcement and rises sharply just before the next one becomes available, exactly as with exam-eve cramming.

section: Educational Psychology · Ch7 — Reinforcement Schedules (Complete: FR/VR/FI/VI)
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: A teacher gives surprise (pop) quizzes at unpredictable times, sometimes twice a week, sometimes not for three weeks. Because students never know when the next quiz will happen, they tend to maintain steady, consistent study habits. This pattern illustrates a:

options.option_text: Variable-interval schedule (reinforcement after an unpredictable TIME period)

explanation: Variable-interval schedules reinforce the first response after an unpredictable time period, producing slow, steady response rates without the scalloping seen in fixed-interval schedules — since the learner can never predict exactly when the next opportunity arrives, unlike a fixed weekly test.

section: Educational Psychology · Ch7 — Reinforcement Schedules (Complete: FR/VR/FI/VI)
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: Which pair correctly distinguishes 'ratio' schedules from 'interval' schedules?

options.option_text: Ratio schedules reinforce based on the NUMBER of responses made; interval schedules reinforce based on the amount of TIME elapsed
Ratio schedules are based on time; interval schedules are based on number of responses
Both ratio and interval schedules are based purely on time, with no difference
Ratio and interval schedules apply only to classical conditioning, never operant conditioning

explanation: The core distinction: ratio schedules (fixed/variable) trigger reinforcement after a certain COUNT of responses; interval schedules (fixed/variable) trigger reinforcement after a certain amount of TIME has passed (with at least one response required) — both are operant conditioning concepts, unrelated to classical conditioning.
